name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Discoveries and contributions of cell biologists

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists listed in Column I with their respective discoveries or contributions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek I. Omnis cellula-e cellula
B. Robert Brown II. Fluid mosaic model of plasma membrane
C. Rudolf Virchow III. First saw and described a live cell
D. Singer and Nicolson IV. Discovery of the nucleus

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's contribution
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell using his improved microscope lenses.

Step 2: Identify Robert Brown's contribution
Robert Brown discovered the cell nucleus in 1831 as a distinct internal structure of the cell.

Step 3: Identify Rudolf Virchow's contribution
Rudolf Virchow in 1855 proposed the concept of Omnis cellula-e cellula, explaining that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Step 4: Identify Singer and Nicolson's contribution
Singer and Nicolson in 1972 proposed the fluid mosaic model, describing the structure and quasi-fluid dynamics of the plasma membrane.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek corresponds to first seeing and describing a live cell; Robert Brown corresponds to the discovery of the nucleus; Rudolf Virchow corresponds to Omnis cellula-e cellula; and Singer and Nicolson corresponds to the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Storage content of different leucoplast types

questiontext.text:
Match the plastids given in Column I with their stored reserve materials or functional pigments given in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Amyloplast I. Traps light energy with chlorophyll and carotenoids
B. Elaioplast II. Stores carbohydrates such as starch
C. Aleuroplast III. Stores oils and fats
D. Chloroplast IV. Stores proteins

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the function of amyloplasts
Amyloplasts are non-pigmented leucoplasts specialised for the storage of carbohydrates, such as starch in potato tubers.

Step 2: Determine the function of elaioplasts
Elaioplasts are colourless leucoplasts that synthesise and store lipids, oils, and fats.

Step 3: Determine the function of aleuroplasts
Aleuroplasts are specialized leucoplasts that store nutrient proteins.

Step 4: Determine the function of chloroplasts
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments dedicated to trapping solar radiant energy for photosynthesis.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Amyloplast pairs with storage of carbohydrates such as starch; Elaioplast pairs with storage of oils and fats; Aleuroplast pairs with storage of proteins; and Chloroplast pairs with trapping light energy using chlorophyll and carotenoids.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Characteristic cell shapes across various cell types

questiontext.text:
Match the cell types listed in Column I with their characteristic shapes shown and described in the chapter in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Red blood cells I. Amoeboid
B. White blood cells II. Long and narrow
C. Columnar epithelial cells III. Round and biconcave
D. Mesophyll cells IV. Round and oval

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the shape of human red blood cells
Human erythrocytes are enucleated, round, and biconcave discs, approximately 7.0 µm in diameter, providing optimal surface area for gas exchange.

Step 2: Identify the shape of white blood cells
Leukocytes are amoeboid in shape, enabling diapedesis and pseudopodial movement through tissues.

Step 3: Identify the shape of columnar epithelial cells
Columnar epithelial cells are tall, pillar-like, long, and narrow structures with basally located nuclei.

Step 4: Identify the shape of mesophyll cells
Photosynthetic mesophyll cells of plant leaves are typically round and oval parenchymatous cells containing numerous chloroplasts.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Red blood cells match with round and biconcave; White blood cells match with amoeboid; Columnar epithelial cells match with long and narrow; and Mesophyll cells match with round and oval.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Surface and accessory structures of bacteria

questiontext.text:
Match the bacterial structures in Column I with their corresponding descriptions or roles in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Flagellum I. Small bristle-like fibres helping in attachment to rocks and host tissues
B. Pili II. Small circular DNA outside genomic DNA conferring antibiotic resistance
C. Fimbriae III. Filamentous organ composed of filament, hook, and basal body for motility
D. Plasmid IV. Elongated tubular structures made of a special protein

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterize the bacterial flagellum
Bacterial flagella are filamentous extensions originating from the cell wall, composed of a basal body, hook, and filament, and serve specifically in cell motility.

Step 2: Characterize bacterial pili
Pili are elongated tubular appendages composed of specialized pilin protein; they do not mediate locomotion.

Step 3: Characterize bacterial fimbriae
Fimbriae are numerous small bristle-like protein fibres sprouting from the cell surface that facilitate attachment to substrates, stream rocks, and host tissues.

Step 4: Characterize bacterial plasmids
Plasmids are extrachromosomal, self-replicating, closed circular double-stranded DNA molecules that impart unique phenotypic advantages, such as antibiotic resistance.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Flagellum corresponds to the filamentous organ composed of filament, hook, and basal body for motility; Pili corresponds to elongated tubular structures made of a special protein; Fimbriae corresponds to small bristle-like fibres aiding attachment; and Plasmid corresponds to small circular extrachromosomal DNA conferring antibiotic resistance.

questiontext.text:
Match the endomembrane organelles listed in Column I with their specific cellular functions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum I. Digestion of macromolecules at acidic pH
B. Golgi apparatus II. Transport of ions against gradient in plant cells
C. Lysosomes III. Synthesis of lipids and steroidal hormones
D. Vacuolar tonoplast IV. Packaging and modification of glycoproteins and glycolipids

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER)
The SER lacks surface ribosomes and serves as the primary site for lipid biosynthesis, phospholipid formation, and synthesis of steroidal hormones in animal cells.

Step 2: Analyze the Golgi apparatus
The Golgi cisternae receive materials from the endoplasmic reticulum via transport vesicles, modify them, and act as key sites for assembling glycoproteins and glycolipids before secretion or sorting.

Step 3: Analyze lysosomes
Lysosomes are membrane-delimited vesicles rich in hydrolytic enzymes (such as lipases, proteases, carbohydrases, and nucleases) that function optimally under acidic pH to degrade macromolecules.

Step 4: Analyze the tonoplast of plant vacuoles
The tonoplast is the semi-permeable limiting membrane of the plant vacuole that facilitates active transport of ions against concentration gradients into the vacuolar sap.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum matches with synthesis of lipids and steroidal hormones; Golgi apparatus matches with packaging and modification of glycoproteins and glycolipids; Lysosomes match with digestion of macromolecules at acidic pH; and Vacuolar tonoplast matches with transport of ions against gradient in plant cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Centromere position and chromosome classification morphology

questiontext.text:
Match the chromosome types given in Column I with their centromeric positions and arm lengths in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Metacentric I. Terminal centromere at the tip of the chromosome
B. Sub-metacentric II. Centromere close to end forming one extremely short and one very long arm
C. Acrocentric III. Middle centromere forming two equal arms
D. Telocentric IV. Centromere slightly away from middle forming one shorter and one longer arm

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterize metacentric chromosomes
Metacentric chromosomes possess a median centromere situated in the exact middle, producing two equal chromosome arms.

Step 2: Characterize sub-metacentric chromosomes
Sub-metacentric chromosomes possess a centromere displaced slightly away from the center, giving rise to one shorter arm (p arm) and one longer arm (q arm).

Step 3: Characterize acrocentric chromosomes
Acrocentric chromosomes have the centromere positioned sub-terminally very close to one end, yielding an extremely short arm and an unusually long arm.

Step 4: Characterize telocentric chromosomes
Telocentric chromosomes possess a strictly terminal centromere located at the extreme tip.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Metacentric matches with middle centromere forming two equal arms; Sub-metacentric matches with centromere slightly away from middle forming one shorter and one longer arm; Acrocentric matches with centromere close to end forming one extremely short and one very long arm; and Telocentric matches with terminal centromere at the tip.

questiontext.text:
Match the structural components of eukaryotic motility and cytoskeletal complexes in Column I with their organization patterns in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Ciliary axoneme I. Nine peripheral triplets linked to a central proteinaceous hub
B. Centriole II. Disc-shaped protein structures on the sides of the centromere
C. Basal body III. Nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a central pair
D. Kinetochores IV. Centriole-like anchor structure from which cilia and flagella emerge

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the ciliary axoneme
The eukaryotic axoneme of cilia and flagella is composed of longitudinal microtubules organized into a classic \(9+2\) array: nine peripheral doublets encircling a central singlet pair.

Step 2: Evaluate the centriole
Centrioles display a cartwheel architecture consisting of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplets of tubulin fibrils connected via radial protein spokes to a central hub (\(9+0\) array).

Step 3: Evaluate the basal body
Basal bodies are centriole-derived structures positioned at the cell cortex that anchor cilia and eukaryotic flagella.

Step 4: Evaluate kinetochores
Kinetochores are specialized disc-shaped trilaminar protein plaques located on the lateral surfaces of chromosomal centromeres where spindle fibres attach during cell division.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Ciliary axoneme matches with nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a central pair; Centriole matches with nine peripheral triplets linked to a central proteinaceous hub; Basal body matches with centriole-like anchor structure from which cilia and flagella emerge; and Kinetochores match with disc-shaped protein structures on the sides of the centromere.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Membrane transport mechanisms across plasma membrane

questiontext.text:
Match the transport processes across the plasma membrane in Column I with their fundamental mechanisms and characteristics in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Simple diffusion I. Energy-dependent movement of ions against concentration gradient using ATP
B. Osmosis II. Transport of polar molecules across nonpolar lipid bilayer via carrier proteins without energy
C. Facilitated transport III. Spontaneous passive flux of neutral solutes down their concentration gradient
D. Active transport IV. Passive diffusion of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate simple diffusion
Neutral solutes cross the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer directly down their concentration gradient (from higher to lower concentration) without requiring carrier proteins or cellular energy expenditure.

Step 2: Evaluate osmosis
Osmosis is the net diffusion of water (solvent) across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of higher water concentration to lower water concentration.

Step 3: Evaluate facilitated transport
Because lipid bilayers are nonpolar and impermeable to polar molecules, polar solutes require membrane carrier proteins to facilitate their passage along the concentration gradient without ATP expenditure.

Step 4: Evaluate active transport
Active transport transports ions or molecules against their concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration), consuming metabolic energy in the form of ATP, exemplified by the \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) ATPase pump.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Simple diffusion matches with spontaneous passive flux of neutral solutes down concentration gradient; Osmosis matches with passive diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane; Facilitated transport matches with transport of polar molecules across lipid bilayer via carrier proteins without energy; and Active transport matches with energy-dependent movement of ions against concentration gradient using ATP.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Specialized non-endomembrane compartments and inclusion structures

questiontext.text:
Match the intracellular structures and compartments in Column I with their specific characteristics in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Gas vacuoles I. Non-membrane bound site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis in the nucleoplasm
B. Chromatophores II. Flattened membranous sacs arranged in stacks in the chloroplast stroma
C. Nucleolus III. Membranous pigment-containing cytoplasmic extensions in cyanobacteria
D. Thylakoids IV. Non-membrane bound inclusion structures found in photosynthetic bacteria

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify gas vacuoles
Gas vacuoles are proteinaceous, non-unit-membrane-bound structures found in photosynthetic prokaryotes (blue-green, purple, and green photosynthetic bacteria) that provide buoyancy.

Step 2: Identify chromatophores
Chromatophores are specialized internal membranous extensions of the plasma membrane in cyanobacteria that harbor photosynthetic pigments.

Step 3: Identify the nucleolus
The nucleolus is a dense, non-membrane-delimited spherical region inside the nucleoplasm that acts as the primary site for the transcription and processing of precursor ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

Step 4: Identify thylakoids
Thylakoids are discrete, flattened membranous cisternae organized into stacks (grana) within the stroma of chloroplasts, housing chlorophyll pigments for photosynthetic light reactions.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Gas vacuoles correspond to non-membrane bound inclusion structures found in photosynthetic bacteria; Chromatophores correspond to membranous pigment-containing cytoplasmic extensions in cyanobacteria; Nucleolus corresponds to non-membrane bound site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis in the nucleoplasm; and Thylakoids correspond to flattened membranous sacs arranged in stacks in the chloroplast stroma.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_THE_UNIT_OF_LIFE_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Chemical constituents of cell walls and envelope layers

questiontext.text:
Match the extracellular or envelope layers in Column I with their characteristic biochemical compositions or structural roles in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Algal cell wall I. Calcium pectate layer that cements neighbouring plant cells together
B. Middle lamella II. Cellulose, galactans, mannans, and calcium carbonate
C. Plant cell wall III. Cytoplasmic channels traversing cell walls connecting adjacent cells
D. Plasmodesmata IV. Cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and proteins

Select the correct match from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the composition of algal cell walls
The cell wall of algae exhibits a distinct composition containing cellulose, galactans, mannans, and minerals such as calcium carbonate.

Step 2: Determine the composition of the middle lamella
The middle lamella is an extracellular cementing layer predominantly composed of calcium pectate that binds adjacent plant cells together.

Step 3: Determine the composition of higher plant cell walls
Higher plant cell walls consist of cellulose microfibrils embedded in an amorphous matrix of hemicellulose, pectins, and structural proteins.

Step 4: Determine the role of plasmodesmata
Plasmodesmata are microscopic channels traversing the primary cell walls and middle lamellae, creating cytoplasmic continuity between adjoining plant cells.

Step 5: Final conceptual answer
Algal cell wall pairs with cellulose, galactans, mannans, and calcium carbonate; Middle lamella pairs with calcium pectate layer that cements neighbouring plant cells together; Plant cell wall pairs with cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and proteins; and Plasmodesmata pairs with cytoplasmic channels traversing cell walls connecting adjacent cells.
